prompt.context: The salted food division at Nabisco has been steadily losing market share over the past two years, from a high of 20% to the current level of 18%. Profits as a percentage of sales, however, have been growing.
prompt.question: What could be causing this?

clarifying_info.a: The largest competitors are two multinational consumer products companies that feature complete lines of snack foods. Together they have about 50% of market share.

clarifying_info.q: How does Nabisco differentiate itself from competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Nabisco's sales reps are regarded as the best in the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Has Nabisco changed its product line?
clarifying_info.a: No, there have been no changes to the product line.

clarifying_info.q: What sales channels does Nabisco use?
clarifying_info.a: Products are primarily sold in large grocery store chains and convenience stores.

clarifying_info.q: Why was the sales force cut?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force was cut to reduce costs, but the number of outlets remained unchanged.

clarifying_info.q: What caused the change in the marketing budget?
clarifying_info.a: The changes come from reduced trade promotions.

clarifying_info.q: How often does the sales force visit customers?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force visits each customer at least once per quarter.
Promotions usually occur at the end of each quarter.

clarifying_info.q: What is the impact of promotions?
clarifying_info.a: Promotions are required for end-of-aisle displays and advertising space.

framework: External Factors: Assess competitor and market dynamics that may be causing market share loss
Competitor dynamics: Have existing players gained share? Have new players entered?
Market dynamics: Is the total market growing faster than Nabisco's sales, causing dilution?
Internal Factors: Assess whether Nabisco's own decisions are driving the share loss
Revenue drivers: Has product mix, pricing, or distribution changed?
Cost structure: Has Nabisco cut costs in ways that affect revenue-generating activities (marketing, sales force)?
Synthesis: Connect internal cost cuts to external market share impact

questions.prompt: Examine Exhibits 1 and 2. What do they reveal about Nabisco's situation?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will note that if total market is growing but Nabisco's sales are growing more slowly (or flat), the market share loss is due to market growth outpacing Nabisco's growth — not necessarily an absolute sales decline. This sets up the question of why Nabisco is failing to capture market growth.

questions.prompt: Examine Exhibit 3. What changes in cost structure stand out, and what might they imply?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will identify that Marketing spend dropped from 18% to 16% and Sales force spend dropped from 9% to 7% — the two line items most directly tied to winning and retaining shelf space and customers. Pre-tax profit rose from 14% to 17%, confirming profits improved as costs were cut. The candidate should hypothesize that these cost cuts may have sacrificed revenue-generating activities.

math.setup: Compare cost line items as % of selling price: Current vs. Two Years Ago
math.answer: Marketing and sales force costs fell by 2pp each; pre-tax profit improved by 3pp. The savings came primarily from reduced trade promotions and headcount, which improved short-term profitability at the expense of market-facing activities.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors could explain why a company's market share declines while its profit margin improves?

categories.name: Cost-cutting trade-offs
ideas: Reduced trade promotions lead to loss of end-of-aisle display space
Smaller sales force means less frequent customer visits and weaker relationships
Fewer promotions means reduced advertising space in stores

categories.name: Competitor actions
ideas: Existing competitors increased their promotional spend, capturing Nabisco's shelf space
New entrants attracted customers with introductory promotions
Competitors launched new products or line extensions

categories.name: Market dynamics
ideas: Market is growing overall but Nabisco is not capturing new growth
Nabisco's product line has not changed while category innovation continues
Grocery and convenience channels are highly promotion-driven; without promotions, share erodes

categories.name: Channel dynamics
ideas: Large grocery chains and convenience stores rely on trade promotions to allocate shelf space
End-of-aisle placement is negotiated via promotional dollars
Reducing trade promotions removes Nabisco from premium shelf positions

recommendation: Nabisco's market share decline is driven by internal cost-cutting decisions — specifically, reductions in trade promotions and sales force — which have reduced shelf space and in-store visibility in grocery and convenience channels
While short-term profitability has improved (14% → 17% pre-tax), this improvement is likely unsustainable as continued share erosion will eventually reduce absolute profit dollars

Nabisco should reinvest in trade promotions to recapture shelf space and end-of-aisle displays, and evaluate whether the sales force reduction can be partially reversed or compensated through more targeted customer engagement
risks: Continued market share loss in a growing market means missed revenue opportunity and potentially permanent loss of shelf positioning
The profitability improvement masks a deteriorating competitive position — costs savings are finite while share losses can compound
Restoring trade promotions may require above-market spending to win back shelf space already ceded to competitors
next_steps: Quantify the revenue impact of lost market share versus the cost savings achieved
Benchmark trade promotion spend against key competitors to assess whether Nabisco is at a structural disadvantage
Evaluate the ROI of restoring targeted trade promotions in highest-volume grocery and convenience accounts
Assess product innovation pipeline — the unchanged product line in a category with routine new products and line extensions is a separate risk
